faults.detail: The mix-up is 'a tilted square corner is not a right angle'. The first task, "Banao square", on an upright dot grid lets the child build an upright square, so the belief never has to be tested. The second task does use a tilted square frame, but it is a bracing task ("Brace lagao: hilna nahi chahiye", "HILTA HAI"/"MAZBOOT HAI") about rigidity, not about whether its corners are right angles. Nothing asks the child to judge or build a right angle that is turned, so a child holding the mix-up is never shown where it goes wrong.
The round has 2 challenges (a square and a rigid frame), but the counter shows a total of 0. The screen disagrees with its own round.
This is English completion feedback in a Hinglish piece (lang "hinglish"), and "Blueprints" is not a word a class-4 child would know.
At 412 px the third header pill runs past the card's right edge: the "s" of "60s" is clipped and the timer bar is cut off.

notes: The sub-title "Frame ko dhyan se jodo" does not say what the second task wants. I could not tell from the first screen alone whether the engine shows the brace instruction when that challenge starts, so I did not count it.

faults.where: piece-l1366.png, rule chip "Daura 1 sam" and falling hexagon "43"
faults.detail: On the 1366 px first screen the rule chip "Daura 1 sam" sits on top of the falling "43" hexagon: the chip's lower edge covers the hexagon's top point, so the two overlap.

notes: Every round uses lo 0, hi 70 with a random seed, and the spec does not show which numbers fall. So the packet cannot show whether 0 (or 10, 20) actually appears in an even/odd round, which is where the zero-not-even mix-up would go wrong. The mix-up check was not counted for this reason. The rules (even/odd on 0-70) and the labels 'sam'/'visham' are correct.

faults.where: rounds[0]: customers[0] items "Ticket" price 1250 (shown "1 × ₹12.50"), pays 2000 (shown "Diye ₹20"), mode "change"
faults.detail: The mix-up is lining up numbers of different lengths from the left (e.g. 48 written under the 32 of 3256). The piece is one change-making round, ₹20 − ₹12.50, where the child picks notes and coins to make the change. There is no column work and no 2-digit number set against a 4-digit one. A child holding the belief could still build ₹7.50 from coins, so the belief never shows. The numbers are also rupee-and-paise decimals, not the 4-digit whole-number addition and subtraction in the topic's cards (e.g. "2345 + 1432", "3256 + 48").
Misspelt: the Hinglish imperative is "gino" (count), not "ginno".
The round has 1 customer waiting (customers has 1 entry), so the count should read 0/1. "0/0" disagrees with the round.
